### FN-LOG-001: LOG(number, base) always divides RN53(RN64(LN(number) / LN(base))), even for base 10

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0 builds 20131 and 20430, omitting base (LOG(number)) routes to LOG10 and returns
exact integers on powers of 10 (LOG(1000) = 3, LOG(0.1) = -1), whereas passing an explicit base
(including base = 10 or 2) evaluates the staged x87 quotient RN53(RN64(LN(number) / LN(base))).
Consequently, LOG(1000, 10) returns 2.9999999999999996 (0x4007ffffffffffff) and LOG(0.1, 10)
returns -0.9999999999999998 (0xbfeffffffffffffe). LOG(1, base < 1) publishes +0, and base = 1
returns #DIV/0!. All 25,233 full-bank LOG rows match.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `LOG(1000, 10)` | number `1000.0` (`0x408f400000000000`); base `10.0` (`0x4024000000000000`) (cells) | `2.9999999999999996` (`0x4007ffffffffffff`) | `3.0` (`0x4008000000000000`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, workbook compatibility 2; CPU not recorded |
| `LOG(0.1, 10)` | number `0.1` (`0x3fb999999999999a`); base `10.0` (`0x4024000000000000`) (cells) | `-0.9999999999999998` (`0xbfeffffffffffffe`) | `-1.0` (`0xbff0000000000000`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, workbook compatibility 2; CPU not recorded |
| `LOG(1000)` | number `1000.0` (`0x408f400000000000`) (cells) | `3.0` (`0x4008000000000000`) | — | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, workbook compatibility 2; CPU not recorded |

Correct value: Exact base-10 logarithm of 1000 is 3.
Correct value: Exact base-10 logarithm of 0.1 is -1 (0.1 in binary64 differs from 1/10 by
5.55e-18, giving log10(binary64(0.1)) = -1 + 2.41e-17, which rounds to -1.0 in binary64).

Basis (measured): Measured in CalcFunc-Evidence
runs/w111-log-omitted-base-20260929/answers-log.json.gz (Excel 16.0 build 20430) and matched on

### FN-LOG10-001: LOG10 executes x87 FLDLG2 + FYL2X directly, differing from LOG(x, 10)

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0 build 20430, LOG10(x) rejects x <= 0 with #NUM! and executes the x87 FLDLG2 +
FYL2X fused logarithm stored to binary64. Unlike LOG(x, 10) (which divides two x87 LN calls),

### FN-LOGNORM.DIST-001: LOGNORM.DIST and LOGNORMDIST use CRT ln(x) for the CDF and exp_of_sum in LN(sigma), LN(sqrt(2pi)), LN(x) order for PDF

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to LOGNORM.DIST,
LOGNORMDIST.

In Excel 16.0 builds 20131 and 20430, LOGNORM.DIST(x, mean, standard_dev, cumulative) and
LOGNORMDIST(x, mean, standard_dev) (cumulative only) require x > 0 and standard_dev > 0. The
CDF evaluates NORM.S.DIST((crt_log(x) - mean) / standard_dev, TRUE) using CRT ln(x) rather than
Excel's scalar LN(x) (distinguished at oc3066), while the PDF forms half_square =
RN53(RN64(d*d) / RN64(sigma*sigma)) / 2 with d = RN53(RN64(excel_log(x) - mean)) and evaluates
excel_exp_of_sum(half_square, [excel_log(sigma), LN_SQRT_2PI, excel_log(x)]), flushing
subnormals to 0. All 7,809 LOGNORM.DIST and 3,299 LOGNORMDIST full-bank rows match.

### FN-LOOKUP-001: LOOKUP chooses search axis by cols > rows in 2-arg form, requires a 1-row/1-col result_vector in 3-arg form, and returns #VALUE! on blank vectors

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, LOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_vector, [result_vector]) bisects in
two-argument form along the first row (returning from the last row) when columns > rows and
along the first column (last column) otherwise. In three-argument form it returns #N/A if
result_vector has both >1 rows and >1 columns, if either vector is a multi-area reference, or
if a result_vector array is shorter than the matched index; returns #VALUE! if lookup_vector or

### FN-LOWER-001: LOWER leaves letters above U+FFFF alone, and a combining mark stops the final sigma

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.* Applies to LOWER, PROPER.

LOWER did not change the Deseret capital U+10400, a cased letter above U+FFFF, either alone or
inside other text: LOWER("A𐐀Σ") is "a𐐀ς", where the Greek capital sigma at the end becomes
the final form. Greek sigma depends on what follows: followed by a full stop it takes the final
form ς, and followed by a combining mark, U+0300 or U+0301, it takes the medial form σ. PROPER
treats a character above U+FFFF as a word boundary, so PROPER("a𐐀b") is "A𐐀B", with the B
capitalised and the Deseret letter unchanged.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LOWER(A1)` | text `𐐀` (cells) | `𐐀` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |
| `LOWER(A1)` | text `A𐐀Σ` (cells) | `a𐐀ς` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |
| `LOWER(A1)` | text `ΑΣ̀` (cells) | `ασ̀` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |
| `LOWER(A1)` | text `ΑΣ.` (cells) | `ας.` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |
| `PROPER(A1)` | text `a𐐀b` (cells) | `A𐐀B` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |
| `PROPER(A1)` | text `aΣ́` (cells) | `Aσ́` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |

Basis (measured): 6 recorded LOWER and 4 recorded PROPER readings, in a workbook at
compatibility version 2.

Inferred, not measured: The readings cover one Deseret letter and two combining marks. That
every letter above U+FFFF and every mark behave the same is inferred.

### FN-MATCH-001: MATCH and VLOOKUP require equal UTF-16 length in non-wildcard exact mode and count wildcard ? in UTF-16 units

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to MATCH, VLOOKUP.

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, MATCH(..., 0) and VLOOKUP(..., FALSE) without wildcards match only
text of the same UTF-16 code-unit length: "SS" does not match "ß" and "ae" does not match "æ",
whereas "e"&UNICHAR(769) (length 2) matches "e"+U+0301 in D2 rather than precomposed "é" in D1.
In wildcard mode, "?" matches one UTF-16 code unit, so surrogate-pair emoji "😀" matches "??"
rather than "?". Both functions read a blank or omitted lookup_value as 0 and reject lookup
strings longer than 255 UTF-16 code units with #VALUE!.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `=MATCH("SS",D5:D16,0)` | as typed | `#N/A` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=VLOOKUP("ae",D7:D16,1,FALSE)` | as typed | `#N/A` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=MATCH("??",{"😀";"a";"ab"},0)` | as typed | `1.0` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=MATCH("?",{"😀";"a";"ab"},0)` | as typed | `2.0` (`0x4000000000000000`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to MDETERM, MMULT.

when any pivot is 0 and #VALUE! for non-square matrices), and MMULT accumulates row-by-column
dot products in binary64 (returning #VALUE! when left columns differ from right rows). Unlike
MINVERSE, neither requires x87 double-rounding to match recorded Excel answers, and both reject
empty, text, or logical matrix entries with #VALUE!.

### FN-MINUTE-001: MINUTE and SECOND add 0.5/86400 (half a second) to the serial before extracting fractional time components

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to MINUTE, SECOND.

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, MINUTE and SECOND round the serial to the nearest second by adding
0.5/86400 before decomposing the fractional day into hours, minutes, and seconds. Thus
MINUTE(0.5 + 1/86400/2) rounds 12:00:00.5 up to 12:00:01 and returns 0, and SECOND(0.5 +
1/86400*1.5) rounds 12:00:01.5 to 12:00:01 or 12:00:02 according to binary64 evaluation,
returning 1.

### FN-MIRR-001: MIRR compounds positive NPV by full cashflow count n rather than n - 1 and diverges up to 9.6 ULP on two-flow calls

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527, MIRR(values, finance_rate, reinvest_rate) computes positive_npv using
NPV's x87-staged loop, multiplies it by pow(1 + reinvest_rate, n) (over all n entries rather
than n - 1), checks a zero finance divisor (#DIV/0!) before final normalization overflow except
when a positive term itself overflows (#NUM!), and takes the (n - 1)-th root via
pow(-grown_positive / finance_pv, 1 / (n - 1)) - 1. Because of the extra divide-and-multiply by
(1 + reinvest_rate) and x87 staging, MIRR({-100, 110}, -1, 0.1) returns 0.09999999999999987
(0x3fb9999999999990), 9.6 ULP below 0.1.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `MIRR({-100, 110}, -1, 0.1)` | value1 `-100.0` (`0xc059000000000000`); value2 `110.0` (`0x405b800000000000`); finance_rate `-1.0` (`0xbff0000000000000`); reinvest_rate `0.1` (`0x3fb999999999999a`) (cells) | `0.09999999999999987` (`0x3fb9999999999990`) | `0.1` (`0x3fb999999999999a`) | Excel 16.0.20527, Windows (bitness and CPU not recorded), en-ZA |

### FN-MOD-001: MOD with tiny operands gives wrong signs and #NUM!, by a rule that fits every recorded row

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

MOD(n,d) takes the exact remainder r of n by d and adds d when their signs differ. Three things
change when r is subnormal and its sign differs from d's. The result is #NUM! when |n/d| is
2^26 or more, or when d's low part under a Veltkamp split at 2^27 + 1 is subnormal. Otherwise,
when |r| is below 2^-1026, the result is |d| + |r| with d's sign: the remainder is added where
it should be taken away. A larger r takes the ordinary step. Any subnormal final result is
#NUM!. So MOD(-(1+121*2^-52)*2^-983, 2^-983) returns +(1+121*2^-52)*2^-983, and MOD(2^-983,
-(1+120*2^-52)*2^-983) returns #NUM!, where the exact answers are ordinary numbers.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `MOD(-1.223247290044572e-296, 1.223247290044539e-296)` | number `-1.223247290044572e-296` (`0x8280000000000079`); divisor `1.223247290044539e-296` (`0x0280000000000000`) (cells) | `1.223247290044572e-296` (`0x0280000000000079`) | `1.2232472900445062e-296` (`0x027fffffffffff0e`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |
| `MOD(1.223247290044539e-296, -1.2232472900445716e-296)` | number `1.223247290044539e-296` (`0x0280000000000000`); divisor `-1.2232472900445716e-296` (`0x8280000000000078`) (cells) | `#NUM!` | `-3.25938553492266e-310` (`0x80003c0000000000`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |

Correct value: MOD(n,d) = n - d*INT(n/d) in exact rational arithmetic; the result is exactly
representable.

Basis (measured): All 152,432 recorded MOD rows match, 4,974 of them rows the ordinary step
misses, and so do 1,128 new Excel readings (build 20527). Those readings overturned an earlier
test on power-of-two divisors: 1E-296 behaves like a power of two and 1E-300 does not.

Inferred, not measured: The rule is what is measured. Reading it as Veltkamp's split, the parts
of a Dekker product of the count and the divisor, is an interpretation: a table over exponent
and trailing zeros puts the boundary between exponents -1000 and -990 and at about 27 trailing
zeros.

Evidence:

- DnaCalc `crates/calc-func/src/catalogue/rounding.rs` at `ab94fb91a5` — the rules in the product; the commit message carries the row counts
- [`content/notes/evidence/2026-11-04/rounding-EVIDENCE.md`](../../content/notes/evidence/2026-11-04/rounding-EVIDENCE.md) — research write-up: full-bank result, the rules, what stays open

### FN-MODE-001: MODE ignores direct text and logicals instead of converting them or giving an error

*Documentation differs from behaviour; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.* Applies to MODE,
MODE.MULT, MODE.SNGL.

MODE, MODE.SNGL and MODE.MULT take only numbers from their arguments, even when text or a
logical is typed directly into the call. A direct "2" or TRUE is not converted, so MODE("2",2)
and MODE(TRUE,1) are #N/A: one number, no repeat. Text that is not a number gives no error
either: MODE("x",2,2) is 2, and MODE("x") is #N/A. Error values do come through: MODE(2,2,A3)
with #DIV/0! in A3 is #DIV/0!, and of two errors the first is returned.

Documentation: Arguments that are error values or text that can't be translated into numbers
cause errors.
(https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/mode-function-e45192ce-9122-4980-82ed-4bdc34973120)

### FN-MROUND-001: MROUND counts a quotient within 5E-15 below a half up

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

MROUND(n,m) forms q = n/m on the x87 unit and stores it to binary64, counts floor(q), adds 1
when 0.5 - frac(q) <= 5E-15, and returns count*m from the x87 unit. A number just below a half
therefore rounds up though it is nearer the lower multiple: 0.499999999999995 with multiple 1
gives 1, and the next binary64 below it gives 0. MROUND(6.05,0.1) stays 6, because its quotient
60.49999999999999 lies 7.1E-15 below the half.

Documentation: MROUND rounds up, away from zero, if the remainder of dividing number by
multiple is greater than or equal to half the value of multiple.
(https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/mround-function-c299c3b0-15a5-426d-aa4b-d2d5b3baf427)

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `MROUND(0.499999999999995, 1)` | number `0.499999999999995` (`0x3fdfffffffffffa6`); multiple `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) (cells) | `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) | `0` (`0x0000000000000000`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |
| `MROUND(0.49999999999999495, 1)` | number `0.49999999999999495` (`0x3fdfffffffffffa5`); multiple `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) (cells) | `0` (`0x0000000000000000`) | — | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |
| `MROUND(0.49999999999999994, 1)` | number `0.49999999999999994` (`0x3fdfffffffffffff`); multiple `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) (cells) | `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) | `0` (`0x0000000000000000`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |

Correct value: The number is nearer to 0 than to 1.

Basis (measured): All 50,782 recorded MROUND rows match this rule. The cut-off lies between the
adjacent binary64 values 4.996E-15 (rounded up) and 5.0515E-15 (rounded down) from 0.5,
measured at floor(q) = 0 over 4,264 rows.

Inferred, not measured: The window is measured between two neighbouring values; that the
constant is the decimal 5E-15 is inferred, as the decimal in that window.

### FN-MULTINOMIAL-001: MULTINOMIAL sums log10(2..=total), subtracts log10(2..=item) in reverse argument order, and rejects total > 170

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; inferred; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527, MULTINOMIAL truncates each admitted argument toward zero (negative gives
#NUM!), rejects total > 170 with #NUM!, accumulates acc = sum_{k=2..=total} excel_log10(k),
then loops over the flattened items in reverse order (last argument first, first argument last)
subtracting excel_log10(2..=item), and finishes with POWER(10.0, acc). Because acc climbs
toward log10(170!) ~ 306.8 before subtracting the item logs back down, rounding at larger
exponents leaves systematic drift (up to 4,672 ULP on single-argument inputs, where acc < 0
also triggers POWER's 1.0 / p reciprocal and even LSBs) and makes MULTINOMIAL non-commutative:
MULTINOMIAL(4, 108) differs from MULTINOMIAL(108, 4) by 107 ULP.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |

### FN-NEGBINOMDIST-001: NEGBINOMDIST evaluates Loader's saddle-point mass times p/(s+f), drifting on exact dyadic rationals at p = 0.25

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20131 and 16.0.20527, the legacy PMF-only NEGBINOMDIST(number_f, number_s,
probability_s) rejects raw number_f < 0 before truncating counts toward zero, requires
truncated s >= 1 and 0 < p < 1 (#NUM! otherwise), preserves subnormal exp(s * ln(p)) at f = 0,
and for f > 0 evaluates the saddle-point binomial mass of s - 1 successes in s + f - 1 trials
with -ln(s + f) in the running exponential followed by stored RN53(RN64(p / (s + f))) (flushed
if subnormal). On exact dyadic rationals =NEGBINOMDIST(10,5,0.25) and =NEGBINOMDIST(1,5,0.25),
Excel is 1 ULP low and 2 ULP high.

### FN-NETWORKDAYS.INTL-001: NETWORKDAYS.INTL checks weekend before the dates, WORKDAY.INTL after them

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.* Applies to NETWORKDAYS.INTL, WORKDAY.INTL.

The two functions read their arguments in different orders. NETWORKDAYS.INTL decodes weekend
first: with #REF! in the cell for start_date and weekend 0, the answer is #NUM!, from the
invalid weekend. WORKDAY.INTL reads start_date first and gives #REF! for the same arguments. An
error held in the weekend cell is also treated differently: with start 2 and second argument 5,
NETWORKDAYS.INTL gives #VALUE! and WORKDAY.INTL gives #NUM!. Neither returns the error itself.
A logical weekend is read as a number: NETWORKDAYS.INTL(2,5,TRUE) is 4, as with weekend 1, and
FALSE is #NUM!, as with weekend 0. WORKDAY.INTL does the same.

### FN-NOMINAL-001: NOMINAL switches between continuous x87 FYL2X/F2XM1 at n <= 2 and stored x87 pow at n >= 3, drifting 22 ULP on 4 periods

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0 builds 20228 through 20527, NOMINAL(effect_rate, npery) truncates npery toward
zero (returning #NUM! for effect_rate <= 0 or truncated npery < 1), computes base = RN53(RN64(1
+ effect_rate)) and reciprocal = 1 / periods, uses register-continuous x87 FYL2X/F2XM1/FSCALE

### FN-NORM.DIST-001: NORM.DIST and NORMDIST densities store x87 z, divide EXP(-z^2/2) by stdev before 1/sqrt(2*pi), and flush subnormals

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to NORM.DIST,
NORMDIST.

In Excel 16.0 builds 20430 and 20527, NORM.DIST(x, mean, stdev, cumulative) and NORMDIST
evaluate cumulative = TRUE as NORM.S.DIST((x - mean) / stdev, TRUE) in binary64, whereas for
cumulative = FALSE they compute z = RN53(RN64(RN53(RN64(x - mean)) / stdev)), square z in x87
(returning #NUM! on overflow), compute EXP(-sq / 2), divide by stdev BEFORE multiplying by
RN(1/sqrt(2*pi)) = 0x3fd9884533d43651, and flush subnormal outputs to +0. Under compat-1,
@NORM.DIST returns #NAME? while NORMDIST remains available.

### FN-NORM.S.DIST-001: NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE) and NORMSDIST(z) scale |z| in stored x87 before ERFC.PRECISE, diverging up to 72 ULP in the tail

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to
NORM.S.DIST, NORMSDIST.

In Excel 16.0.20131 through 16.0.20527, NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE) and NORMSDIST(z) compute z_scaled
= RN53(RN64(|z| * RN(1/sqrt(2)))) and pass it to Excel's ERFC.PRECISE kernel, returning 0.5*Q
for z < 0 and RN53(RN64(1 - 0.5*Q)) for z >= 0, flushing subnormal results to +0.0 (e.g.
NORMSDIST(-37.52) = 0). Because ERFC.PRECISE loses accuracy in the Gaussian tail,
NORM.S.DIST(-10.907735625234475, TRUE) differs by 72 ULP from the true mathematical CDF.

### FN-NORM.S.INV-001: NORM.S.INV uses AS241 tails (p < 0.075 and p > 15/16) and three x87-stored rational/Padé pieces for sqrt(2)*erfinv(2p-1) in between

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; inferred; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to CONFIDENCE,
CONFIDENCE.NORM, LOGINV, LOGNORM.INV, NORM.INV, NORM.S.INV, NORMINV, NORMSINV.

Excel's standard normal inverse (NORM.S.INV and NORMSINV) partitions (0, 1) asymmetrically:
Wichura's AS241 formula runs for p < 0.075 and p > 15/16 using x87 FYL2X + FSQRT stored
sqrt(-ln v), while the middle computes sqrt(2) * erfinv(t) with t = 2*(p - 0.5) across three
pieces: for s = RN(t*t) <= 0.5, a degree-7/7 rational interpolant at the 15 zeros of T15 on [0,
0.73] solved near 100-bit precision; for sqrt(0.5) < |t| <= 0.85, a degree-7/5 rational
interpolant times sqrt(-ln(1 - |t|)); and for 0.85 < t <= 0.875 (p in (0.925, 15/16]), a
degree-9/9 Padé approximant centred at 225/256 solved at 96-bit precision times sqrt(-ln(1 -
t)), storing every Horner product and sum from x87 64-bit precision to binary64.
NORM.INV/NORMINV return mu + sigma*z, LOGNORM.INV/LOGINV return EXP(mu + sigma*z), and
CONFIDENCE/CONFIDENCE.NORM return NORM.S.INV(1 - alpha/2)*sigma/SQRT(size) with stored steps.
See
https://github.com/DnaCalc/DnaCalc/blob/4fb9b728df8a96546ae685589b47e057b7e26771/docs/articles/last-bit-normsinv.md.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Recorded in |

| `=NORM.INV(0.9,40,1.5)` | as typed | `41.9223273483169` (`0x4044f60ed2929d1e`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

### FN-NPER-001: NPER uses exact rate == 0 for linear branch (#DIV/0! when 1 + rate rounds to 1) and x87-stored logs elsewhere

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20131 through 16.0.20527, NPER(rate, pmt, pv, [fv], [type]) takes the linear
branch -(fv + pv) / pmt only at exact rate == 0.0 (returning #DIV/0! if pmt == 0). Any nonzero
rate enters the logarithmic formula using x87 PC64-to-PC53 double-rounded operations and x87
FYL2X logarithms: tiny rates where 1 + rate rounds to 1 return #DIV/0! (such as rate = 1e-300),

### FN-NUMBERVALUE-001: NUMBERVALUE falls back to the host VALUE grammar for letter/digit separators and rounds 15-digit mantissas by reciprocal

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527 (en-ZA), when given a separator outside ".", ",", " ", or U+00A0 on text
its own reader refuses, NUMBERVALUE strips group_separator before the first decimal_separator,
replaces decimal_separator with the host decimal separator, and parses via the host VALUE
grammar (e.g. NUMBERVALUE("%1e3", ".", "e") is 0.13, while NUMBERVALUE("1e-3", "e", ",") is
#VALUE!). On 15-digit mantissas such as "600757912143053e-27", Excel divides by 10^27 rather
than correctly rounding to binary64, differing by 1 ULP on 48 of 366 fn12 pinned rows. In
compatibility-version-1 workbooks, @NUMBERVALUE evaluates to #NAME?.

### FN-OCT2DEC-001: Octal radix converters count leading zeros in the 10-digit limit, check places first, and reject logicals with #VALUE!

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to OCT2BIN, OCT2DEC, OCT2HEX.

In Excel 16.0 builds 20430 and 20527, OCT2BIN, OCT2DEC, and OCT2HEX reject whitespace and
leading signs with #NUM!, reject logical arguments with #VALUE!, count leading zeros toward the
10-character input limit (so OCT2BIN("00000000000") is #NUM!), and treat 10-character octal
inputs whose high bit (2^29) is set as 30-bit two's-complement negatives. OCT2BIN and OCT2HEX
validate an explicit places argument (truncating into 1..=10) before inspecting number.

### FN-ODDFYIELD-001: ODDFYIELD checks frequency before basis, starts from par-100 seed, and stops Newton when |step| <= 1e-10 before updating

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527, ODDFYIELD validates frequency before reading optional basis, rejects zero
date serials and unaligned first_coupon dates (requiring COUPPCD(first_coupon, maturity, freq,
basis) == first_coupon) with #NUM!, allows negative yields while 1 + y/freq > 0, starts from a
schedule-free par-100 seed y_0, and runs up to 100 Newton iterations on ODDFPRICE using the
regular-coupon derivative (omitting the first-period DFC/E factor), returning the iterate
BEFORE updating when |step| <= 1e-10 (or y_100).

### FN-ODDLPRICE-001: ODDLPRICE and ODDLYIELD clamp both dates to 30 on US 30/360 period lengths but keep standard US 30/360 for accrued A

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to ODDLPRICE, ODDLYIELD.

In Excel 16.0.20527, ODDLPRICE and ODDLYIELD walk forward from last_interest to maturity in
coupon-period steps (requiring at most 64 quasi-periods). For day-count basis 0 (US 30/360),
the quasi-period length NL and period interest fraction DCI use a symmetric rule that clamps
both start and end day-31 or last-day-of-February dates to 30 (days360_us_both), whereas
accrued days A use standard US 30/360 (us_30_360), and negative day counts clamp to 0.

### FN-OFFSET-001: OFFSET defaults omitted or blank shifts to 0, extends negative height/width upward/leftward, and gives #REF! for 0

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527, OFFSET(reference, rows, cols, [height], [width]) truncates all four
numeric arguments toward zero, reads omitted or blank rows/cols as 0, returns #REF! when height
or width is exactly 0 (while fractions in (-1, 1) truncate to 0), extends the resulting
reference upward or leftward from the shifted cell when height or width is negative, and
returns #VALUE! for multi-area references or references to closed external workbooks.

### FN-OP_ADD-001: Addition and subtraction double-round through x87 64-bit significand precision and retain computed subnormals

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to OP_ADD,
OP_SUBTRACT.

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, + and - coerce operands left-to-right to numbers and evaluate each
operation at x87 64-bit significand precision (PC64) before rounding to binary64, differing by
1 ULP from IEEE-754 binary64 single rounding on every row of dc6qki_arith rows 25-52 (e.g.
0.9882+0.000000004364549 = 0x3fef9f559d94e3b2 vs nearest ...e3b3). Unlike * and /, + and -
retain computed subnormal results (0 + EXP(-745) = 2^-1074), while parsed subnormal literals
flush to 0.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `=0.9882+0.000000004364549` | as typed | `0.9882000043645489` (`0x3fef9f559d94e3b2`) | `0.988200004364549` (`0x3fef9f559d94e3b3`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=3.262707-0.00005579` | as typed | `3.2626512099999996` (`0x400a19e8e0a9a37c`) | `3.26265121` (`0x400a19e8e0a9a37d`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `="2"+TRUE` | as typed | `3.0` (`0x4008000000000000`) | — | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

Correct value: Exact rational sum of both binary64 operands and decimal literals, rounded to
nearest binary64
Correct value: Exact rational difference of both binary64 operands and decimal literals,
rounded to nearest binary64

Basis (measured): Measured across Excel 16.0.20527.20088 in dc6qki_arith (rows 25-52),
jnt_operators (rows 1-4, 21), and dc-1943 computed-subnormal probes.

### FN-OP_EQUAL-001: Conjoining Hangul jamo do not compare equal to the precomposed syllable

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.* Applies to OP_EQUAL, OP_LESS_THAN.

U+1100 U+1161 is canonically equivalent to the syllable U+AC00 in Unicode, but Excel's
comparison says they are not equal, and the jamo sequence sorts first. The same holds with a
final consonant, U+1100 U+1161 U+11A8 against U+AC01.

| `="각"="각"` | as typed | `FALSE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

### FN-OP_LESS_THAN-001: Punctuation before a Japanese repeat mark sorts one way after a Latin letter, the other after Han

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.* Applies to OP_GREATER_THAN, OP_LESS_THAN.

Comparing a string with punctuation before a repeat or prolonged-sound mark against the same
string without the punctuation, the order depends on the character at the start. After a Latin
letter the punctuated string is smaller: "a-ゝx" < "aゝx". After a Han character it is larger:
"時-ゝx" > "時ゝx". This held for every pair read, with the marks ゝ, 々 and ー and with hyphen-minus,
U+2212 and U+2019 as the punctuation. In all 66 readings the two strings are never equal, and a
string with the mark added sorts after the string without it, after Latin and after Han alike:
"a−ゝ" > "a−".

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `="a-ゝx"<"aゝx"` | as typed | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `="a-ゝx">"aゝx"` | as typed | `FALSE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `="時-ゝx"<"時ゝx"` | as typed | `FALSE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `="時-ゝx">"時ゝx"` | as typed | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `="a−ゝ"<"aゝ"` | as typed | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `="時−ゝ">"時ゝ"` | as typed | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `="a−ゝ">"a−"` | as typed | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `="時−ゝ">"時−"` | as typed | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

Basis (measured): 66 recorded readings of =, < and > on 22 pairs of strings, 11 pairs after 時
and 11 after a.

- Open: The collation rule behind this is not identified, and none is claimed here.

### FN-OP_NEGATE-001: Unary negation coerces text and logicals to numbers and flushes parsed subnormals to +0

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, unary negation (-x) coerces its scalar operand to a number (so -"2"
= -2 and -TRUE = -1, unlike unary +x which leaves text and logicals uncoerced), flushes parsed
subnormal literals to +0 (-1E-309 = 0x0000000000000000, not -0.0), and retains a computed

### FN-OP_UNARY_PLUS-001: Unary + does not coerce text or logicals, turns a blank cell into 0, and retains computed subnormals

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, unary plus (+x) is not numeric coercion: it leaves text and logical
values unchanged (+"2" returns text "2", +TRUE returns logical TRUE, unlike -"2" and -TRUE),
evaluates a blank cell reference to 0 (+Z1 = 0), propagates errors (+#N/A = #N/A), flushes
parsed subnormal literals (+1E-309 = 0), and preserves computed subnormals.

| `=+Z1` | as typed | `0.0` (`0x0000000000000000`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=+1E-309` | as typed | `0.0` (`0x0000000000000000`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

### FN-PDURATION-001: PDURATION evaluates (LN(fv) - LN(pv)) / LN(1 + rate) rather than LN(fv / pv), drifting 22 ULP at 0.025

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0 builds 20326 through 20527, PDURATION(rate, pv, fv) rejects nonpositive rate, pv,
or fv with #NUM! and computes (LN(fv) - LN(pv)) / LN(1 + rate) via Excel's x87 LN chain instead
of LN(fv / pv) / LN(1 + rate). On =PDURATION(0.025,2000,2200), this yields 3.859866162622655
(0x400ee10182bb35e8), 22 ULP above the exact mathematical value. In compatibility version 1,
@PDURATION returns #NAME?.

| `PDURATION(0, 100, 200)` | rate `0.0` (`0x0000000000000000`); pv `100.0` (`0x4059000000000000`); fv `200.0` (`0x4069000000000000`) (cells) | `#NUM!` | — | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit; CPU not recorded |

### FN-PERCENTILE-001: PERCENTILE.EXC rejects k <= 1/(n+1) or k >= n/(n+1) with #NUM!, while .INC/.EXC return #NAME? in compat-1

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to PERCENTILE, PERCENTILE.EXC, PERCENTILE.INC.

In Excel 16.0.20527, PERCENTILE and PERCENTILE.INC interpolate linearly at rank 1 + k*(n - 1)
over [0, 1], whereas PERCENTILE.EXC interpolates at rank k*(n + 1) and returns #NUM! whenever
rank < 1 or rank > n (for example outside (1/(n+1), n/(n+1))). Under compatibility version 1,

### FN-PERCENTOF-001: PERCENTOF requires _xlfn., maps held array or reference errors to #NUM!, and coerces only direct scalars

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, PERCENTOF(data_subset, data_all) requires the _xlfn. prefix in OOXML
(@PERCENTOF without _xlfn. gives #NAME?), divides SUM(data_subset) by SUM(data_all), coerces
direct text and logicals (PERCENTOF("1",4) = 0.25, PERCENTOF(TRUE,4) = 0.25) and omitted
arguments (PERCENTOF(,4) = 0), skips text/logicals inside references or arrays, sums union
areas, returns direct errors directly (#N/A -> #N/A), and maps any error held inside a
reference or array to #NUM! (PERCENTOF(Data!A1:A3,Data!A1:E3) = #NUM! because Data!C1 holds

### FN-PERMUT-001: PERMUT evaluates an ascending x87 double-rounded product from n - k + 1 to n, not n! / (n - k)!

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20131 through 16.0.20527, PERMUT(number, number_chosen) truncates both arguments
toward zero (rejecting n < 0, k < 0, k > n, or overflow with #NUM!) and accumulates the
ascending x87 PC64-to-PC53 double-rounded product acc = RN53(RN64(acc * f)) for f = n - k + 1
..= n. Evaluating n! / (n - k)! instead overflows early for large n and misses PERMUT(61, 20)
by 1 ULP. All 3,432 full-bank PERMUT rows match.

### FN-PERMUTATIONA-001: PERMUTATIONA checks number < 0 before truncation (-1 < number_chosen < 0 becomes 0) and uses decimal 10^k at base 10

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

0 before truncation (so PERMUTATIONA(-0.9999999999999987, 1) is #NUM!), whereas number_chosen
in (-1, 0] truncates to 0 and returns 1. Both arguments are bounded below 2,147,483,647. When

### FN-PHI-001: PHI computes x87 sq = x*x (#NUM! on overflow), EXP(-sq/2) * 0x3fd9884533d43651, and flushes subnormals to +0

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20131 through 16.0.20527, PHI(x) forms sq = RN53(RN64(x * x)) (rejecting overflow
with #NUM!), evaluates e = EXP(-sq / 2), multiplies by the reciprocal constant RN(1/sqrt(2*pi))
= 0x3fd9884533d43651 in x87 (rather than dividing by sqrt(2*pi)), and flushes subnormal results
to +0.0 (so PHI(37.8511319) = 0). Under compat-1, @PHI returns #NAME?.

|---|---|---|---|
| `PHI(0)` | x `0.0` (`0x0000000000000000`) (cells) | `0.3989422804014327` (`0x3fd9884533d43651`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit; CPU not recorded |
| `PHI(37.8511319000002)` | x `37.8511319000002` (`0x4042ecf1e3dd8aa6`) (cells) | `0.0` (`0x0000000000000000`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit; CPU not recorded |
| `=@PHI(0.75)` | as typed | `#NAME?` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

Basis (measured): Measured across Excel 16.0.20131, 20430, and 20527.20088, matching
14,406/14,406 full-bank and 120/120 pinned PHI rows.

### FN-PI-001: PI returns full binary64 pi (0x400921fb54442d18), 7 ULPs above the documented 15-digit decimal

*Documentation differs from behaviour; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

0x400921fb54442d18 (3.141592653589793), which is 7 representable steps above the

### FN-PMT-001: PMT takes ln(1+rate) from a series, and stores its quotient before the rate

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

With RN(v) meaning v rounded to 64 bits on the x87 unit and then stored to binary64, PMT with
fv 0 and type 0 at rates from -1/3 to 1/2 runs: s = rate/(2+rate); L = 2s + 2s*(s^2*T), where T
= 1/3 + s^2/5 + ... + s^20/23 by Horner, all in plain binary64, which is the atanh series for
ln(1+rate) (Abramowitz and Stegun 4.1.27) with the 2s term added last; t = -(nper*L); u =
exp(t) stored; em = RN(RN(RN(u-1)*t)/ln(u)) for |t| < 1, and RN(u-1) otherwise, Kahan's way of
forming expm1; q = RN(pv/em); PMT = RN(q*rate). L is not the correctly rounded logarithm: at
rate 0.05/12 it is 0x3f7107fd59addc8a, one unit below 0x3f7107fd59addc8b, and the common
30-year loan below comes out 1 unit from the correctly rounded payment.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `=PMT(0.05/12,360,200000)` | as typed | `-1073.6432460242781` (`0xc090c692af15f63a`) | `-1073.643246024278` (`0xc090c692af15f639`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

Correct value: mpmath at 800 bits with rate the binary64 0x3f71111111111111 that 0.05/12
evaluates to; correctly rounded.

Basis (measured): For each of 1,184 rates one binary64 L reproduces Excel's em at every nper
(1,622 of 1,622 power-of-two and 1,849 of 1,849 other nper, L taken from nper 1 alone). The
series gives that L at 1,181 rates; the correctly rounded log1p and fdlibm's log1p each give it
at 667. Order and precision of the last two steps: in all 4,802 groups of recorded answers
sharing (rate, nper) with 8 or more pv values, these steps admit one em; a binary64 quotient
leaves 59 groups with none, and binary64 for both steps 111. 720 of 720 fresh type 0 rows over
20 rates, both signs, match (Excel build 20527). Over every recorded PMT row, types and fv
included, 279,887 of 291,978 match.

Inferred, not measured: The range -1/3 to 1/2 is where twelve series terms converge, not a
measured Excel boundary. Rate 0.419, near sqrt(2)-1, misses by 1 unit, so a range reduction may
start there. Negative rates rest on 20 rates' controls and the recorded rows.

- Open: type 1: Excel multiplies q by one stored binary64 K near rate/(1+rate) per rate (pinned at all but one of about 458 recorded rates and at 20 of 20 fresh ones), but K's formula is open: the correctly rounded quotient fits 344 of 458.
- Open: Nonzero fv: the numerator of q is open. The best form tried fits 5,600 of 7,491 rows, and 146 rows admit no binary64 numerator under this order.
- Open: Rates outside -1/3 to 1/2.

### FN-POISSON.DIST-001: Upper-tail incomplete gamma for a <= 20 runs uncontracted Modified Lentz with TINY=1e-30, and poisson_mass switches at <= 1.1

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; inferred; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to CHIDIST,
CHISQ.DIST, CHISQ.DIST.RT, GAMMA.DIST, GAMMADIST, POISSON, POISSON.DIST.

In Excel 16.0.20527, all upper-tail incomplete-gamma calls with a <= 20.0 (both a < 1.0, x >=
1.1 and 1.0 < a <= 20.0, x > a outside finite sums) evaluate the uncontracted Legendre
continued fraction using Thompson-Barnett Modified Lentz from b_0 = 0 (f = c = TINY, d = 0.0)
with Numerical Recipes TINY = 1.0e-30 (0x39b08b2a2c280291), storing each arithmetic operation
to binary64 at x87 PC64, stopping at k > 0 && del == 1.0, and multiplying S(pm * f) directly
without factoring a out of the fraction. At k = 0, c_0 = S(x + S(a / TINY)) rounds a * 10^30 +
x into binary64, so changing TINY to 1e-50 or 1e-100 breaks about half of 10,000 tested rows.
In poisson_mass(a, x), Excel switches between the compensated exponential and Loader's
saddle-point expansion inclusively at x <= 1.1 || a <= 1.1 (0x3ff199999999999a, verified by
single-bit bisection at 1.1 vs next_up(1.1)). POISSON(x, mean, cum) and POISSON.DIST(x, mean,
cum) match across all 278 paired probes, and POISSON.DIST(k, m, TRUE) equals CHIDIST(2*m,
2*(k+1)) and CHISQ.DIST.RT(2*m, 2*(k+1)). See
https://github.com/DnaCalc/DnaCalc/blob/344d70dcea3ea77cbbeee1595f96694630a9610a/docs/articles/last-bit-gamma.md.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POISSON(1, 32.00000000000001, TRUE)` | x `1.0` (`0x3ff0000000000000`); mean `32.00000000000001` (`0x4040000000000001`); cumulative `TRUE` (cells) | `4.1791746312010515e-13` (`0x3d5d68881f1c6f57`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20196, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H with Radeon Graphics |
| `POISSON.DIST(1, 32.00000000000001, TRUE)` | x `1.0` (`0x3ff0000000000000`); mean `32.00000000000001` (`0x4040000000000001`); cumulative `TRUE` (cells) | `4.1791746312010515e-13` (`0x3d5d68881f1c6f57`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20196, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H with Radeon Graphics |
| `GAMMA.DIST(1.1, 4.143399358773536, 1, FALSE)` | x `1.1` (`0x3ff199999999999a`); alpha `4.143399358773536` (`0x401092d74810cc80`); beta `1.0` (`0x3ff0000000000000`); cumulative `FALSE` (cells) | `0.06233902817180819` (`0x3fafeae6ae865147`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20196, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H with Radeon Graphics |

### FN-POWER-001: POWER and ^ return #NUM! for 0^0, allow negative bases when 1/y rounds to an odd 32-bit integer to 15 digits, and double-round 10^126

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to OP_POWER, POWER.

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, POWER(0,0) and 0^0 return #NUM! and POWER(0,-1) returns #DIV/0!. For
a negative base with fractional exponent y, Excel accepts the real root -POWER(|x|, y) when 1/y
rounded to 15 significant decimal digits is an odd signed 32-bit integer ((-8)^(1/3) =
-1.9999999999999998, (-32)^(1/5) = -2, while (-8)^(2/3) = #NUM!). Integer exponents use staged
binary exponentiation and flush subnormals to +0 (2^-1074 = 0), while POWER(10, k)
double-rounds 10^k through 64-bit significand precision, giving 0x5a17a2ecc414a040 at k = 126
(1 ULP above nearest ...a03f).

|---|---|---|---|
| `=POWER(0,0)` | as typed | `#NUM!` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=(-8)^(1/3)` | as typed | `-1.9999999999999998` (`0xbfffffffffffffff`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=(-8)^(2/3)` | as typed | `#NUM!` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=2^-1074` | as typed | `0.0` (`0x0000000000000000`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

### FN-PPMT-001: PPMT is not PMT minus IPMT, and sits further from the exact value than PMT

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.* Applies to PMT,
PPMT.

On the 30-year loan PPMT(0.05/12,k,360,200000), for k from 1 to 12 every PPMT answer is 3 to 5
units above the correctly rounded principal payment, while PMT is 1 unit away. Excel's own
answers do not satisfy the identity: in binary64, PMT - IPMT equals PPMT in 2 of the 12 periods
and PMT - PPMT equals IPMT in 7. So reproducing PPMT from PMT and IPMT misses the last bits.
FN-IPMT-001 gives the route Excel takes instead.

### FN-PRICEMAT-002: PRICEMAT basis 0 applies the 31st rule before the February rule

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

For basis 0, PRICEMAT tests "end on the 31st gives 30" before "start on the last day of
February gives 30"; the US (NASD) 30/360 rule applies the February adjustment first. An issue
on 28 February 2025 and maturity on 31 March 2043 gives DIM 6511, not 6510, and moves the price
at about 1E-5 relative.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PRICEMAT(46376, 52321, 45716, 0.04392789506562811, 0.03266239139487676, 0)` | settlement `46376` (`0x40e6a50000000000`); maturity `52321` (`0x40e98c2000000000`); issue `45716` (`0x40e6528000000000`); rate `0.04392789506562811` (`0x3fa67db79160c3a0`); yld `0.03266239139487676` (`0x3fa0b91ffdb34689`); basis `0` (`0x0000000000000000`) (cells) | `109.22025565957247` (`0x405b4e18ab31a7da`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H |

Basis (measured): One recorded row separates this rule from the standard one: 2,404 of 2,404
against 2,403.

Inferred, not measured: The order of the two tests is taken from the published
ExcelFinancialFunctions getMatFactors rule, which fits; one row cannot pin it alone.

### FN-PROB-001: PROB validates the running stored sum of probabilities against [1 - 4 ULP, 1 + 22 ULP] rather than per-term [0, 1]

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, PROB accumulates the probabilities in input order as binary64
additions and admits any vector whose final sum lies in [1.0 - 4 ULP, 1.0 + 22 ULP]
(0x3feffffffffffffc ..= 0x3ff0000000000016), so compensating negative or >1 entries (such as
{-0.25, 1.25} or {1e16, -1e16, 1}) are accepted whereas reordered {1e16, 1, -1e16} fails with
#NUM!. Non-numeric scalar x_range or prob_range arguments ("2", TRUE, "x") return #DIV/0!.

### FN-PV-001: PV takes the linear branch only at exact rate == 0 and stores x87 (1 + rate) before POWER and annuity discounting

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20131 through 16.0.20527, PV(rate, nper, pmt, [fv], [type]) takes the linear
route -(fv + pmt * nper) only when rate == 0.0 exactly. For nonzero rate it forms base =
RN53(RN64(1 + rate)), computes factor = POWER(base, nper) (returning #DIV/0! when factor == 0),
forms term = RN53(RN64(RN53(RN64((factor - 1) / rate)) * timing)), and evaluates
-RN53(RN64(RN53(RN64(fv + RN53(RN64(pmt * term)))) / factor)). All 1,564 full-bank PV rows
match.

### FN-RAND-001: RAND, RANDARRAY, and RANDBETWEEN set PtgAttrSemi syntactically, and RANDARRAY requires _xlfn.

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to RAND, RANDARRAY, RANDBETWEEN.

In Excel 16.0.20527, RAND(), RANDARRAY([rows], [columns], [min], [max], [whole_number]), and
RANDBETWEEN(bottom, top) all mark the enclosing formula syntactically volatile (PtgAttrSemi)
regardless of whether the call is in a taken branch, and refuse reference-place or call-postfix
uses at entry. RANDARRAY requires the _xlfn. prefix in OOXML (bare @RANDARRAY gives #NAME?),
whereas RAND and RANDBETWEEN need no prefix; degenerate bounds RANDBETWEEN(1,1) and
RANDARRAY(1,1,1,1,TRUE) deterministically return 1.

### FN-REGEXTEST-001: In REGEXTEST, \w takes combining marks, dot refuses CR, and case folding reaches into ranges

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

Some regular expression details in REGEXTEST differ from a plain reading. \w matches a
combining mark (U+0301) and connector punctuation (U+203F), so it is not limited to letters,
digits and underscore. Dot does not match CR as well as LF: REGEXTEST("a"&CHAR(13)&"b","a.b")
is FALSE. \d does not match a Han character. With case_sensitivity 1, folding applies inside a
character class range: É matches [é-é] and Σ matches [α-ω]. It also covers the non-ASCII
partners of ASCII letters: the Kelvin sign U+212A matches k and long s U+017F matches s. ß
matches its capital U+1E9E, and a Deseret letter above U+FFFF matches its other case.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REGEXTEST(A1, A2, 1)` | text `É`; pattern `[é-é]`; case_sensitivity `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) (cells) | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |
| `REGEXTEST(A1, A2, 1)` | text `Σ`; pattern `[α-ω]`; case_sensitivity `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) (cells) | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |
| `REGEXTEST(A1, A2, 0)` | text `́`; pattern `\w`; case_sensitivity `0` (`0x0000000000000000`) (cells) | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |
| `REGEXTEST(A1, A2, 0)` | text `‿`; pattern `\w`; case_sensitivity `0` (`0x0000000000000000`) (cells) | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |
| `REGEXTEST(A1, A2, 0)` | text `a, CR (U+000D), b`; pattern `a.b`; case_sensitivity `0` (`0x0000000000000000`) (cells) | `FALSE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |
| `REGEXTEST(A1, A2, 1)` | text `K`; pattern `k`; case_sensitivity `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) (cells) | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |
| `REGEXTEST(A1, A2, 1)` | text `ſ`; pattern `s`; case_sensitivity `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) (cells) | `TRUE` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, workbook compatibility version 2 |

Basis (measured): 12 recorded REGEXTEST readings, in a workbook at compatibility version 2.

Inferred, not measured: The readings cover the characters named here. That \w follows the
Unicode Mn and Pc categories in general, and that ranges fold by simple case folding in
general, is inferred.

- Open: Reversed or very wide caseless ranges, and other newline characters, have not been read.

### FN-REGISTER.ID-001: REGISTER.ID is macro-sheet-only (refused on worksheets) and matches procedure names case-sensitively in XLM

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527 (64-bit), REGISTER.ID(module_text, procedure, [type_text]) is valid only on
Excel 4.0 macro sheets (XLM): assigning any REGISTER.ID formula to a worksheet cell throws
0x800A03EC, and opening a saved package containing it fails with 0x800A03EC. Under
Application.ExecuteExcel4Macro, REGISTER.ID requires at least 2 arguments, matches module names
case-insensitively (KERNEL32.DLL == Kernel32) and exported procedure names case-sensitively
(getcurrentprocessid fails with #VALUE!), and returns a numeric process-dependent registration
ID.

### FN-ROMAN-001: ROMAN truncates toward zero, returns empty text for 0, and maps form TRUE/blank to 0 and FALSE to 4

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527, ROMAN(number, [form]) truncates number toward zero into 0..=3999
(returning empty text "" for 0 and #VALUE! outside 0..=3999) and simplifies subtractive pairs
according to form in 0..=4 (returning #VALUE! outside 0..=4). An omitted, blank, or TRUE form

### FN-ROUND-001: ROUND counts digits in 32 bits, and the count wraps

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

ROUND cuts num_digits toward zero to a 32-bit integer D, limited to +/-2147483647, and keeps k
= D + e + 1 significant digits, where e is the decimal exponent of |number| and the sum is
computed in 32 bits. k of 15 or more keeps the 15-digit reading of the number; k below 0 gives
0. A large positive num_digits therefore wraps to no digits at all: for a number near 1.1E14,
2147483617 returns the number and 2147483635 returns 0. The boundaries move by exactly -e on
both the +2^31 and -2^31 sides, for e from -308 to 308. num_digits of 2^31 or more acts as
+2147483647 and -2^31 or less as -2147483647.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ROUND(-112500000000000, 2147483635)` | number `-112500000000000` (`0xc2d9945ca2620000`); num_digits `2147483635` (`0x41dffffffcc00000`) (cells) | `0` (`0x0000000000000000`) | `-112500000000000` (`0xc2d9945ca2620000`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |
| `ROUND(-112500000000000, 2147483617)` | number `-112500000000000` (`0xc2d9945ca2620000`); num_digits `2147483617` (`0x41dffffff8400000`) (cells) | `-112500000000000` (`0xc2d9945ca2620000`) | — | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |

Correct value: -112500000000000 is an integer, so rounding it to any non-negative number of
places returns it.

Basis (measured): Under the family rules the recorded rows match ROUND 36,821 of 36,945,
ROUNDUP 52,022 of 52,841, ROUNDDOWN 59,182 of 59,995 and TRUNC 50,504 of 51,317, with no row
lost and each remaining failure classified in the write-up. The wrap boundary was read at every
decimal exponent in the recorded rows.

### FN-ROUND-002: The rounding functions read 15 digits first, so ROUNDDOWN can round up

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.* Applies to ROUND,
ROUNDDOWN, ROUNDUP, TRUNC.

Before choosing a digit these functions read the number to 15 significant digits on the x87
unit: with e the decimal exponent and n = 14 - e, y = RN64(|x| * 10^n), or RN64(|x| / 10^-n)
when n is negative, while 10^|n| is exact in 64 bits (|n| <= 27). A half in y goes up for
ROUNDDOWN, ROUNDUP and TRUNC and down for ROUND. So digits beyond the 15th are lost even when
the requested precision keeps them: ROUND(-1594628480062905,14) loses its last digit, and
ROUNDDOWN(283025097725723.5,0) returns 283025097725724, larger than its input.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ROUND(-1594628480062905, 14)` | number `-1594628480062905` (`0xc316a939806956e4`); num_digits `14` (`0x402c000000000000`) (cells) | `-1594628480062900` (`0xc316a939806956d0`) | `-1594628480062905` (`0xc316a939806956e4`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H |
| `ROUNDDOWN(283025097725723.5, 0)` | number `283025097725723.5` (`0x42f0168ea69971b8`); num_digits `0` (`0x0000000000000000`) (cells) | `283025097725724` (`0x42f0168ea69971c0`) | `283025097725723` (`0x42f0168ea69971b0`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H |

Correct value: An integer rounded to 14 places is itself.
Correct value: ROUNDDOWN drops the fraction .5.

Basis (measured): Under the family rules the recorded rows match ROUND 36,821 of 36,945,
ROUNDUP 52,022 of 52,841, ROUNDDOWN 59,182 of 59,995 and TRUNC 50,504 of 51,317, with no row
lost and each remaining failure classified in the write-up.

- Open: How the scale is formed for |n| > 27: a single correctly rounded 64-bit power and the chained multiplications tried do not fit; 123 ROUND, 548 ROUNDUP, 556 ROUNDDOWN and 555 TRUNC rows remain.
- Open: The reading step itself: one control at n = -10 misses the single RN64 step by just over half a unit, so that step is an approximation of the real one even for |n| <= 27. It stays because it gains rows and loses none.

Evidence:

- DnaCalc `crates/calc-func/src/catalogue/rounding.rs` at `ab94fb91a5` — the rules in the product; the commit message carries the row counts
- [`content/notes/evidence/2026-11-04/rounding-EVIDENCE.md`](../../content/notes/evidence/2026-11-04/rounding-EVIDENCE.md) — research write-up: full-bank result, the rules, what stays open

### FN-ROUND-003: Near DBL_MAX, ROUND returns NaN bit patterns that Excel treats as numbers

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.* Applies to ROUND,
ROUNDDOWN, ROUNDUP, TRUNC.

ROUND of a number near 1.8E308 can return a binary64 with an all-ones exponent field. A decimal
result of 2^1024 or more keeps its 53-bit significand, and its exponent is carried into the
exponent field without a check, so the bits are a NaN. ROUND, ROUNDDOWN and TRUNC return those
bits; ROUNDUP gives #NUM!. The recorded rows hold 430 such ROUND rows, 102 ROUNDDOWN and 95
TRUNC, and all 627 follow this. Even ROUND(DBL_MAX,0), whose answer is DBL_MAX, returns
0x7ff000000000000a. The cell shows 2E+308 or 1.8E+308, and a pattern with its sign bit set
shows 2E+308 too, with no minus. ISNUMBER gives TRUE, ISERROR FALSE, TYPE 1, ERROR.TYPE #N/A;
A1=A1 and A1>0 are TRUE. =A1, N(A1), MAX(A1), ABS(A1) and IFERROR(A1,...) pass the pattern on,
as does =-A1 with its sign unchanged. Arithmetic on it (A1+0, A1*1, A1-A1, SUM, ROUND) gives
#NUM!, and TEXT(A1,"0") gives #VALUE!. Saved to .xlsx, each such cell is written as the error
#NUM!; reopened, the cells read #NUM! until a full recalculation brings the patterns back.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ROUND(1.7976931348623157E+308, 0)` | number `1.7976931348623157e+308` (`0x7fefffffffffffff`); num_digits `0` (`0x0000000000000000`) (cells) | `NaN bit pattern, shown as 1.8E+308` (`0x7ff000000000000a`) | `1.7976931348623157e+308` (`0x7fefffffffffffff`) | Excel 16.0 build 20527, Windows; bitness and CPU not recorded in this reading |
| `ROUND(1.7976931348623157E+308, -307)` | number `1.7976931348623157e+308` (`0x7fefffffffffffff`); num_digits `-307` (`0xc073300000000000`) (cells) | `NaN bit pattern, shown as 1.8E+308` (`0x7ff005419221015d`) | `#NUM!` | Excel 16.0 build 20527, Windows; bitness and CPU not recorded in this reading |
| `ROUND(1.7976931348623157E+308, -308)` | number `1.7976931348623157e+308` (`0x7fefffffffffffff`); num_digits `-308` (`0xc073400000000000`) (cells) | `NaN bit pattern, shown as 2E+308` (`0x7ff1ccf385ebc8a0`) | `#NUM!` | Excel 16.0 build 20527, Windows; bitness and CPU not recorded in this reading |

Correct value: DBL_MAX is an integer, so rounding it to 0 places returns it.
Correct value: The rounded value exceeds the largest binary64; Excel reports overflow in its
own arithmetic as #NUM!.

Basis (measured): One Excel workbook read cell by cell through Value2 on 2026-11-04, saved,
reopened and recalculated; rows from the rounding write-up, 627 of 627.

Inferred, not measured: That one decimal-to-binary conversion routine is the source of all
these patterns is inferred from the exponent-overflow encoding.

- Open: How these patterns sort among themselves and with other numbers, and display width, are not recorded.

### FN-ROUND-004: ROUND takes ties away from zero on the 15-digit reading, so 1.005 rounds up

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

A tie in ROUND goes away from zero, not to even: ROUND(2.5,0) is 3 and ROUND(-2.5,0) is -3. The
tie is judged on the 15-digit reading of FN-ROUND-002, not on the stored value. So 1.005 and
2.675, whose binary64 values lie just below the decimal tie, count as ties: ROUND(1.005,2) is
1.01 and ROUND(2.675,2) is 2.68, where rounding the stored value would give 1 and 2.67.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `=ROUND(2.5,0)` | as typed | `3` (`0x4008000000000000`) | — | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=ROUND(-2.5,0)` | as typed | `-3` (`0xc008000000000000`) | — | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=ROUND(2.675,2)` | as typed | `2.68` (`0x400570a3d70a3d71`) | `2.67` (`0x40055c28f5c28f5c`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=ROUND(1.005,2)` | as typed | `1.01` (`0x3ff028f5c28f5c29`) | `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

Correct value: The stored value lies below the decimal tie, so the nearest multiple of 0.01 is
the lower one; nearest binary64.

### FN-ROUNDUP-001: ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN and TRUNC read num_digits from its low 16 bits

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.* Applies to
ROUNDDOWN, ROUNDUP, TRUNC.

ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN and TRUNC take the digit count from the low 16 bits of the integer part of
|num_digits|, with the sign of num_digits. If |num_digits| is 2^32 or more, or those low bits
are 32768 or more, the truncation happens at 100 places (10^-100, or 10^100 for a negative
count). So 65536 acts as 0, 65537 as 1, 32768 to 65535 as 100, and -2147483748, whose low 16
bits are 100, as -100. In the out-of-range case ROUNDUP adds no unit for a positive count, and
gives #NUM! for a negative count when a digit is dropped.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ROUNDUP(1.234567890123456e-200, 65536)` | number `1.234567890123456e-200` (`0x166e3d71f622be8f`); num_digits `65536` (`0x40f0000000000000`) (cells) | `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) | `1.234567890123456e-200` (`0x166e3d71f622be8f`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |

### FN-ROUNDUP-002: ROUNDUP adds its unit in binary64, one bit from the decimal answer

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

ROUNDUP forms the ROUNDDOWN result, converts it to binary64, converts one unit 10^-p to
binary64, and adds the two on the x87 unit, storing the sum to binary64. The sum need not be
the binary64 value nearest the decimal answer, so ROUNDUP(-1.125,2) is -1.1300000000000001 and
ROUNDUP(3.535,2) is 3.5399999999999996. The difference shows when the result is compared with a
typed 3.54.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ROUNDUP(-1.125, 2)` | number `-1.125` (`0xbff2000000000000`); num_digits `2` (`0x4000000000000000`) (cells) | `-1.1300000000000001` (`0xbff2147ae147ae15`) | `-1.13` (`0xbff2147ae147ae14`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H |
| `ROUNDUP(3.535, 2)` | number `3.535` (`0x400c47ae147ae148`); num_digits `2` (`0x4000000000000000`) (cells) | `3.5399999999999996` (`0x400c51eb851eb851`) | `3.54` (`0x400c51eb851eb852`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H |

Correct value: The decimal answer has a nearest binary64 value; rounding away from zero at 2
places gives that value.

Basis (measured): Under the family rules the recorded rows match ROUND 36,821 of 36,945,
ROUNDUP 52,022 of 52,841, ROUNDDOWN 59,182 of 59,995 and TRUNC 50,504 of 51,317, with no row
lost and each remaining failure classified in the write-up.

Evidence:

- DnaCalc `crates/calc-func/src/catalogue/rounding.rs` at `ab94fb91a5` — the rules in the product; the commit message carries the row counts
- [`content/notes/evidence/2026-11-04/rounding-EVIDENCE.md`](../../content/notes/evidence/2026-11-04/rounding-EVIDENCE.md) — research write-up: full-bank result, the rules, what stays open

### FN-ROUNDUP-003: At tiny magnitudes ROUNDUP may add no unit, and the two signs differ

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

ROUNDUP adds no unit when the unit itself is below the normal range, whichever the sign. For a
positive number it also adds none when the 15-digit reading, as binary64, lies less than
2^-1026 above the truncation; negative numbers have no such distance. So
ROUNDUP(1.0001086461844975E-307,307) is 1E-307 and ROUNDUP(-1.0001086461844975E-307,307) is
-2E-307, with the same digits dropped. At -1.2225E-307 and 308 places the unit, 1E-308, is
subnormal, and the answer stays at -1.2E-307.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ROUNDUP(1.0001086461844975e-307, 307)` | number `1.0001086461844975e-307` (`0x0031fa982c40c60e`); num_digits `307` (`0x4073300000000000`) (cells) | `1e-307` (`0x0031fa182c40c60d`) | `2e-307` (`0x0041fa182c40c60d`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |
| `ROUNDUP(-1.2225073858507202e-307, 308)` | number `-1.2225073858507202e-307` (`0x8035fa182c40c60e`); num_digits `308` (`0x4073400000000000`) (cells) | `-1.2e-307` (`0x80359283684dba77`) | `-1.3e-307` (`0x80375eb9065434ab`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |
| `ROUNDUP(1.0000000022250739e-300, 307)` | number `1.0000000022250739e-300` (`0x01a56e1fc3c5c026`); num_digits `307` (`0x4073300000000000`) (cells) | `1.0000001000000001e-300` (`0x01a56e1fe6ed23b2`) | — | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |

Correct value: The number has a nonzero digit past 307 places, so rounding away from zero at
307 places gives 2E-307; nearest binary64.
Correct value: The number has a nonzero digit past 308 places, so rounding away from zero at
308 places gives -1.3E-307; nearest binary64.

Basis (measured): ROUNDUP rows match under these rules as counted in FN-ROUND-001. In the 1,148
recorded rows nearest the 2^-1026 boundary this quantity has 1 violation, itself an artefact of
how the row was classified; the exact value, the reading and x minus the truncation give 54 to
547. The opposite-sign pair is a reading from Excel build 20527.

- Open: 14 ROUNDUP rows of tiny magnitude stay unmatched, in the near-tie class of FN-ROUND-002.

### FN-ROW-001: ROW returns a vertical array up to 1,048,576 rows on multi-row areas and #REF! on multi-area unions

### FN-RRI-001: RRI runs the raw x87 EXP((1/nper)*LN(fv/pv)) - 1 chain (skipping nper == 1), drifting 298 ULP on RRI(96,10000,11000)

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0 builds 20228 through 20527, RRI(nper, pv, fv) rejects nper < DBL_MIN before
checking pv == fv (with DAZ normalization, so equal negative pv and fv return +0), rejects pv
== 0 or opposite nonzero signs with #NUM!, returns fv / pv - 1 directly at nper == 1, and
otherwise evaluates exp(RN53(RN64((1 / nper) * ln(fv / pv)))) - 1 via the raw x87 chain
(bypassing POWER's 0.5 sqrt shortcut). Subtracting 1 near 1 loses bits, putting
=RRI(96,10000,11000) 298 ULP below exact. Under compat-1, @RRI returns #NAME?.

### FN-SEQUENCE-001: SEQUENCE truncates dimensions, advances by stored additions, and puts #NUM! only in overflowing cells

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527, SEQUENCE(rows, [columns], [start], [step]) coerces its arguments in
formula order, truncates positive fractional dimensions (requiring rows*columns >= 1, else
#CALC!; negative or invalid dimensions give #VALUE!), and advances each cell in row-major order
by one stored binary64 addition cur = cur + step rather than start + k*step. When accumulation
overflows finite binary64, only the overflowing cells become #NUM! while earlier cells retain
finite values.

|---|---|---|---|
| `=CONCAT(SEQUENCE(2,3))` | as typed | `123456` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |
| `=CONCAT(SEQUENCE(3,1,10,-2))` | as typed | `1086` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

### FN-SERIESSUM-001: SERIESSUM rejects logicals with #VALUE!, zeroes fractional powers of negative x, and flushes subnormal powers

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527, SERIESSUM(x, n, m, coefficients) rejects logical values with #VALUE! in
every argument (including inside the coefficients array/range), treats an omitted or blank
scalar x as 0, evaluates each power term x^(n + i*m) using POWER's kernel except substituting 0
(rather than #NUM!) when x < 0 and n + i*m is non-integral, flushes subnormal power terms to 0
before multiplying by the coefficient (even when the coefficient is 0), and multiplies each
term in x87 PC64 before accumulating.

### FN-SHEET-001: SHEET and SHEETS return #N/A for invalid non-error arguments and evaluate to #NAME? in compatibility version 1

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to SHEET, SHEETS.

### FN-SINH-001: SINH splits at |x| = 1 between internal Kahan expm1 and x87-stored EXP difference, differing by 1 ULP on small inputs

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0 builds 20326 through 20527, SINH(number) evaluates (expm1(x) - expm1(-x)) / 2
using Excel's internal binary64 Kahan expm1 for |x| < 1, switches at |x| >= 1 to
RN53(RN64(EXP(x) - EXP(-x))) / 2, and rejects overflow above ln(DBL_MAX) (~709.78) with #NUM!.
Because Excel builds expm1 from its x87 EXP/LN primitives, SINH(0.013409894617721019) differs
by 1 ULP from mathematical sinh(x). Of 33,551 full-bank SINH rows, 33,547 match and 4 differ by
1 ULP.

### FN-SLOPE-001: SLOPE pairs known_y's then known_x's, skips non-numeric positions, and centers with two-pass means

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0 builds 20131 and 20527, SLOPE(known_y's, known_x's) validates singletons in
formula order (returning #VALUE! for a single blank reference before inspecting the other
argument), returns #N/A on shape mismatch, skips positions where either argument holds text,
logical, or blank, and computes sum((x - mean_x)*(y - mean_y)) / sum((x - mean_x)^2) from

### FN-SORTBY-001: SORTBY orders keys by Excel collation (including Japanese iteration marks) and preserves input order on primary ties

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, SORTBY sorts by blank < number < text < logical < error, using
Excel's 15-digit numeric comparison (except IEEE total order on qualified overflow values >=
2^1023) and case-insensitive collation on text, and merges adjacent ascending runs stably. Thus
"Σ", "ς", and "σ" tie in primary weight and retain input order (1|2|3), "i" < "ı" < "İ" < Greek
< emoji "😀", and the Japanese kanji iteration mark "時々" sorts between prefix "時" and "時a".

| `=TEXTJOIN("\|",FALSE,SORTBY({1;2;3;4;5;6;7},{"Σ";"ς";"σ";"i";"İ";"ı";"😀"}))` | as typed | `4\|6\|5\|1\|2\|3\|7` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

### FN-SQRT-001: SQRT is rounded twice, once to 64 bits and once to 53

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

The worksheet SQRT is RN53(RN64(sqrt(x))): the root is rounded to the x87 unit's 64-bit
significand and then stored to binary64. On inputs where that double rounding lands differently
from a single rounding, Excel takes the double-rounded value: SQRT(0.9999999999999999) is 1. A
subnormal written to a cell reads back as 0, so the 0 for the smallest subnormal below may
record that and not SQRT.

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SQRT(0.9999999999999999)` | number `0.9999999999999999` (`0x3fefffffffffffff`) (cells) | `1` (`0x3ff0000000000000`) | `0.9999999999999999` (`0x3fefffffffffffff`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |
| `SQRT(1.7976931348623157e+308)` | number `1.7976931348623157e+308` (`0x7fefffffffffffff`) (cells) | `1.3407807929942597e+154` (`0x5ff0000000000000`) | `1.3407807929942596e+154` (`0x5fefffffffffffff`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |
| `SQRT(5e-324)` | number `5e-324` (`0x0000000000000001`) (cells) | `0` (`0x0000000000000000`) | — | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, CPU not recorded in this capture |

Correct value: Exact square root at 800 bits, correctly rounded.

Basis (measured): 41,897 of 41,897 distinct normal positive recorded rows match. On the 164
rows where double and correct rounding differ, Excel follows double rounding every time. The
subnormal row is 1 row, and no read-back of its input is recorded.

Evidence:

- DnaCalc `crates/calc-func/src/ported/sqrt_fn.rs`, excel_sqrt_staged at `b5ce0759bc` — the kernel in the product
- CalcFunc-Evidence `runs/w111-broad-20260929/answers/answers-sqrt.json.gz`, w111broad-20260929-SQRT-00016 at `4d5320dfdc` (readings)
- CalcFunc-Evidence `runs/w111-broad-20260929/answers/answers-sqrt.json.gz`, w111broad-20260929-SQRT-00025 at `4d5320dfdc` (readings)

### FN-SQRTPI-001: SQRTPI uses CRT pow(n*pi, 0.5) not IEEE sqrt, returns #NUM! for n*pi > DBL_MAX, and rejects logicals

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0 builds 20026, 20430, and 20527, SQRTPI(number) rejects logicals with #VALUE!,
rejects number < 0 with #NUM!, multiplies number * pi in binary64 (returning #NUM! once number
* pi overflows DBL_MAX, starting at 0x7fd45f306dc9c883), and evaluates CRT pow(number * pi,
0.5) rather than IEEE sqrt. At =SQRTPI(1), Excel returns 1.7724538509055159
(0x3ffc5bf891b4ef6a), 1 ULP below exact sqrt(pi); at 0x7fd45f306dc9c882 it returns

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

### FN-SUM-001: SUM evaluates all direct-argument errors before held reference/array errors, and overflow does not mask later errors

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, SUM checks direct scalar arguments (including text-to-number
coercion #VALUE!) in argument order before reporting any error held inside a reference or array
argument, so =SUM(A1:B2,"a") and =SUM({1,#REF!},"a") both return #VALUE! even when B1 holds
#N/A. Among held errors, SUM follows argument order, and a numeric overflow to #NUM! does not
stop reading later arguments, so =SUM(9.99999999999999E+307,9.99999999999999E+307,B1) returns
#N/A.

| `=SUM(9.99999999999999E+307,9.99999999999999E+307,B1)` | as typed | `#N/A` | Excel 16.0.20527.20088 Current Channel, Windows 64-bit (NT 10.0.26200), x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, en-ZA |

### FN-SUM-002: SUM, AVERAGE, and AVERAGEA apply Excel's 50-exponent cancellation snap once at the final numeric addition

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; inferred; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to AVERAGE,
AVERAGEA, SUM.

In Excel 16.0.20527 (dc-ss3b), SUM snaps its final result to +0 when the last left partial
sum's binary exponent exceeds the sum's binary exponent by at least 50 (so SUM(0.1,0.2,-0.3)
returns +0 rather than 2^-54). A trailing numeric 0 counts as the final addition and suppresses
the snap (SUM(0.1,0.2,-0.3,0) returns 2^-54, 0x3c90000000000000), whereas trailing cell text,
logicals, and blanks are skipped and do not suppress it. AVERAGE and AVERAGEA apply the same
rule to their numerator before dividing by the count; SUMPRODUCT does not snap.

Basis (inferred): Measured across 98+ Excel 16.0.20527 probes in dc-ss3b
(docs/research/sum-cancellation-2026-11-12.md) covering scales 2^-900 to 2^900, exponent gaps
49 vs 50, zero vs skipped tails, and AVERAGE/AVERAGEA/SUMPRODUCT controls; full-bank SUM
(1,211/1,211), AVERAGE (1,222/1,222), and AVERAGEA (1,212/1,212) remain matched.

Inferred, not measured: That the shared post-addition snap uses the exact 50-exponent threshold
across every binade is inferred from the dc-ss3b power-of-two boundary sweeps; the raw probe
JSON files were archived to R2 (research/round53/20261112-fn2-0327/) rather than committed to
git.

- Open: Archive a representative subset of raw dc-ss3b SUM(0.1,0.2,-0.3) and SUM(0.1,0.2,-0.3,0) Excel readings in git so repros can cite a repository path directly.

Evidence:

- DnaCalc `docs/research/sum-cancellation-2026-11-12.md` at `4fb9b728df` — dc-ss3b probe predictions, results, and sibling controls in Excel 16.0.20527
- DnaCalc `crates/calc-func/src/catalogue/aggregate.rs`, sum; mean at `4fb9b728df` — Shared adjust_final_sum call in SUM, AVERAGE, and AVERAGEA
- DnaCalc `crates/calc-func/tests/f1_stats.rs`, sum_adjusts_the_last_numeric_addition at `4fb9b728df` — Regression tests covering all dc-ss3b probe behaviours

### FN-SUMPRODUCT-001: SUMPRODUCT reads direct text as 0 and rejects omitted args, unions, and single blank refs with #VALUE!; PRODUCT/SUMSQ/SUMPRODUCT flush subnormals to +0

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.* Applies to PRODUCT, SUMPRODUCT, SUMSQ.

In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, SUMPRODUCT evaluates direct scalar text to 0 (SUMPRODUCT("3") = 0)
and returns #VALUE! for an omitted argument (SUMPRODUCT(A1:A2,) = #VALUE!), a multi-area union
(SUMPRODUCT((A1,A7)) = #VALUE!), or a single blank cell reference (while multi-cell ranges read
blanks as 0). By contrast, PRODUCT skips omitted arguments (PRODUCT(2,) = 2) and returns

### FN-SYD-001: SYD admits negative cost and fractional periods, forms (life + 1) - per in x87, and flushes subnormal denominators

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0 builds 20430 and 20527, SYD(cost, salvage, life, per) admits negative cost and
fractional per/life while rejecting salvage < 0, life <= 0, per <= 0, or per > life (by >=
DBL_MIN) with #NUM!. It evaluates denominator = life * (life + 1) / 2 in x87 (flushing
nonfinite or subnormal denominators to 0 and returning #DIV/0!), stores basis = cost - salvage

### FN-TAN-001: TAN reduces arguments with x87 FPREM1(x, FLDPI/2) and rejects |x| >= 2^27 with #NUM!, drifting at large inputs

*Excel differs from the mathematical answer; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0.20131 through 16.0.20527, TAN(x) rejects |x| >= 2^27 (134,217,728) with #NUM! and
otherwise evaluates FPREM1(x, FLDPI/2), FPTAN, and -1/tan(r) in extended precision on odd
quadrants before a single store to binary64. Because reduction uses the 64-bit x87 FLDPI/2
constant rather than exact pi/2, large arguments drift from mathematical tan(x):

### FN-TANH-001: TANH divides SINH(x) by an expm1-based denominator for |x| < 1 (and COSH(x) for |x| >= 1) in x87, saturating to +/-1

*Detail for matching Excel's bits; measured; recorded 2026-11-22.*

In Excel 16.0 builds 20326 through 20527, TANH(number) computes RN53(RN64(SINH(x) /
denominator)), where denominator is (RN53(RN64(expm1(x) + expm1(-x))) + 2) / 2 in x87 for |x| <
1 (distinct from public COSH) and COSH(x) for |x| >= 1, saturating to +/-1.0 on large |x| via
SATURATE_SIGN. Of 39,028 full-bank TANH rows, 39,025 match and 3 differ by 1 ULP.

### FN-TBILLEQ-001: For bills longer than 182 days TBILLEQ is a quadratic, not the documented formula

*Documentation differs from behaviour; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

When DSM is above 182, TBILLEQ does not use the documented formula. It uses the bond-equivalent
quadratic (-t + sqrt(t^2 - (2t-1)(1 - 1/p))) / (t - 1/2), with t = DSM/365 and p = price/100.
At DSM 366, a bill across a 29 February, t is 1 and not 366/365. The square root is taken in
extended precision and stored, RN53(RN64(sqrt)); the rest is binary64. For the row below, DSM
203, the documented formula gives 0.244038 and Excel 0.241103. Excel's bits are 22 units below
the correctly rounded quadratic because of that staging.

Documentation: TBILLEQ is calculated as TBILLEQ = (365 x rate)/(360-(rate x DSM)); the page
does not mention 182 days.
(https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/tbilleq-function-2ab72d90-9b4d-4efe-9fc2-0f81f2c19c8c)

| Call | Inputs (binary64) | Excel | Correct value | Recorded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `TBILLEQ(40633.25, 40836.25, 0.21193100748125787)` | settlement `40633.25` (`0x40e3d72800000000`); maturity `40836.25` (`0x40e3f08800000000`); discount `0.21193100748125787` (`0x3fcb208e2511f676`) (cells) | `0.24110326418450792` (`0x3fcedc78c550cec1`) | `0.24110326418450853` (`0x3fcedc78c550ced7`) | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H |
| `TBILLEQ(53886, 54252, 0.4522540814812992)` | settlement `53886` (`0x40ea4fc000000000`); maturity `54252` (`0x40ea7d8000000000`); discount `0.4522540814812992` (`0x3fdcf1bb1a5c75f4`) (cells) | `0.7211303677406913` (`0x3fe7137ffe3328bc`) | — | Excel 16.0 build 20430, Windows 64-bit, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H |

Correct value: mpmath at 800 bits: the exact quadratic at the binary64 inputs, correctly
rounded.

Basis (measured): 2,400 of 2,400 recorded rows with the stored square root; 2,399 without it.
All 33 recorded rows with a number answer at DSM 366 fit t = 1, and none of the 17 of them in
the run below fits 366/365.

### FN-TEXT-001: Locale-tagged month, weekday and era names in TEXT follow their own table

*Quirk; measured; recorded 2026-11-04.*

With a locale tag in the format, TEXT's names differ from common locale data. [$-407] (German)
gives mmm for March as Mrz, while mmmm gives März. [$-411] (Japanese) gives mmm as a bare
number, 1, while mmmm gives 1月. [$-419] (Russian) capitalises mmmm (Январь) but not mmm (янв),
and capitalises ddd (Ср) but not dddd. The first year of the Reiwa era prints as 1, not 元年; g,
gg and ggg give R, 令 and 令和, switching on 2019-05-01.
